progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: the five parts in order ("Some Really Cool Elephants Run"); negative feedback opposes a change; positive feedback strengthens a change until an end point (blood clotting); the regulated variable is inside the body. From b02: nerve impulses are the fast neural pathway; hormones travel in the blood. From b03 (route level only: "Trace the response to rising glucose" and "Explain the reciprocal response to falling glucose"): beta cells release insulin when glucose rises; liver, muscle and fat cells take up glucose and the liver stores glycogen; alpha cells release glucagon when glucose falls, and the liver breaks glycogen down to release glucose. From b04 (route level only): not used. From b05: ABA closes stomata under water stress. Not assumed: baroreceptor (the card supplies its meaning: "stretch receptors"), cardiovascular centre (supplied), ethylene (supplied: "a gas").
progression.startsWith: An unfamiliar system described in words. The video opens: Feedback loop questions turn up in HSC Biology again and again, in different disguises.
progression.stopsAfter: constructing the blood pressure loop from a description (stimulus: blood pressure falls; receptors: baroreceptors in the aorta and carotid arteries; control centre: cardiovascular centre in the medulla oblongata; effectors: heart and arterioles; response: a faster, stronger heartbeat and narrower arterioles raise blood pressure back towards normal; a minus on the return arrow) and predicting that damaged baroreceptor nerves leave pressure low after standing; reading a glucose and insulin graph after a meal (glucose peaks first at 30 minutes, insulin at 45 minutes because the rise in glucose is the stimulus for insulin release; from 45 to 120 minutes insulin makes liver, muscle and fat cells take up glucose and store glycogen, glucose falls to about its fasting value and insulin falls with it; after the dip below fasting at 150 minutes, alpha cells release glucagon and the liver releases glucose from glycogen); identifying ethylene ripening as positive feedback and explaining that glucagon raising a fallen glucose level is negative feedback because the response opposes the change.
progression.nextLesson: investigate plant water loss in a practical (route entry bio-m8-p02).

teaching.task: When an exam gives you an unfamiliar system, a glucose graph or a list of processes, how do you build the loop, read it off the data, and tell negative feedback from positive?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why the response must name the variable (it is what the loop regulates; 2b, 2d); how the effectors raise pressure (more blood pumped each minute, narrower arterioles; 2b, the 2021 and 2025 marker comments on causal paths); why a cut link leaves pressure low (no signal reaches the control centre; 2c); why insulin peaks after glucose (glucose is its stimulus; 3b); why glucose falls and insulin falls with it (target cells take up glucose, and the falling stimulus lowers secretion; 3c); why glucose rises after the dip (glucagon, liver glycogen; 3c); why R is positive (each round adds more ethylene; 4b); why Q is negative despite the rise (the response opposes the fall; 4c).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Feedback loop questions turn up in HSC Biology in different disguises, and most come down to three moves: build the loop in order, read it off a graph, and tell negative feedback from positive. Q1 (blood pressure falling on standing up quickly) takes each part from the stem: the fall in pressure as stimulus, the baroreceptors, the cardiovascular centre in the medulla, the heart and arterioles as effectors, and a response written as the change in the variable, pressure rising back, with a minus on the return arrow; damaged baroreceptor nerves cut the loop, so pressure stays low and the person may faint; the classic slip ends at the effector with the heart beats faster. Q2 (blood glucose and insulin after a meal) reads the peaks off the axes, glucose at thirty minutes and insulin at forty-five, as the stimulus and the response that follows it, explains the fall from forty-five to one hundred and twenty minutes as insulin making liver, muscle and fat cells take up and store glucose with insulin easing as glucose falls, and explains the late rise from glucagon and the liver, which the graph does not show; the slip says insulin breaks down glucose. Q3 (ABA closing stomata, glucagon in a long run, ethylene ripening bananas) tests each process by whether the response opposes or strengthens the change, picks ethylene ripening as positive feedback, and corrects a student who calls the glucagon loop positive because glucose goes up; the slip reads positive as goes up. A decision board closes: five parts in order with the response as a change in the variable, find the stimulus first on a graph, and compare the response with the original change.
teaching.openingDecision: Feedback loop questions turn up in HSC Biology again and again, in different disguises. Most of them come down to three moves. Build the loop in order, read it off a graph, and tell negative feedback from positive. Here are three HSC-style questions. Pause and try each one, then we'll work through it together.
teaching.understandingCheck: Three, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a). Nothing answer-bearing during the holds.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (2017, `docs/production/programme/syllabus/bio-2017-y12.json`, p 56; practice and transfer only, first coverage stays with b01 to b05): B8-IQ1-01: "construct and interpret negative feedback loops that show homeostasis by using a range of sources, including but not limited to: (ACSBL101, ACSBL110, ACSBL111)" with the listed examples "temperature (ACSBL098)" and "glucose". Q1 is construct (a written description of an unseen system); Q2 is interpret (a glucose and insulin graph, the listed "glucose" example); Q3 is interpret by classifying (negative against positive, across a plant, a glucose and a fruit process). "Range of sources": a written description (Q1), a two-line graph (Q2), three short process descriptions (Q3). B8-IQ1-02 (recalled, not taught): "internal coordination systems that allow homeostasis to be maintained, including hormones and neural pathways" (Q1's nerve impulses, Q2's hormones) and "mechanisms in plants that allow water balance to be maintained" (Q3's process P).

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in g01's layout: top-left the question card (stem, data and demands as an exam prints them, with the "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience" tag), readable through the whole question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("Build a loop", "Read a glucose graph", "Negative or positive?"), hidden during each attempt. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used (no givens card). Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Q1's working is b01's `LoopRing`, filling slot by slot with small plates (`m8-heart-v1.png`, `b3a2-brain-v1.png`) and short labels, then one link cut for the prediction. Q2's working is the coded `lineGraph` with two y axes (glucose and insulin), peak markers and reading guides, with `m8-pancreas-v1.png` and `m8-skeletal-muscle-v1.png` small beside it. Q3's working is three process strips (P, Q, R), each a mini two-slot loop (change → response) with its return arrow taking a minus or a plus, beside its plate (`b2b-prop-new-plant-v1.png`, `m8-pancreas-v1.png`, the new banana pair). No people, hands or faces: the person in Q1 and the adult in Q2 are words only; the body is never outlined. Coded elements are limited to loops, graphs, arrows, chips, tags, answer boxes and the decision board. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): besides the question strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; each working tag fades when the next cue lands. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on as an empty five-slot loop ring, a blank two-line graph and two return arrows marked minus and plus draw in the working area; each question opens on a fresh board with the type badge hidden while the worded card writes beside its small plates; the walkthrough shrinks the card to a strip, lights the type badge and underlines each given as it is used; the loop ring draws large and fills one slot per cue as signal pulses travel round, then a link cut mark stops the pulse and the downstream slots grey; the effector chip slides into its slot to show where it belongs; the graph enlarges, peak markers drop to the axes and the line segments brighten on their cues beside the pancreas, liver and muscle plates; three process strips draw with their plates, each gaining a minus or plus on its cue, and the student's up arrow is set against the stimulus arrow; each question ends with its classic slip chip taking a scribble cross; the decision board becomes two columns, each row lighting on its cue with its question badge; scene crossfade with settle.
